rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The religious scholars are truth’s defenders in the struggle of good and evil: they enjoined virtue, forbade vice, endured miscreants’ harms, and defended the innocent, deserving the turret’s vantage.
rows.anchor: proponents of the truth in the conflict between good and evil and those who enjoined the virtue and forbade vice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greetings show the righteous see the promised final scenes before entering Paradise, so they can witness God’s promise fulfilled.
rows.anchor: they will not yet have entered it but would be contenders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling themselves candidates for mercy expresses humility: even amid God’s favours, they do not claim certainty of salvation.
rows.anchor: they would humble consider themselves to be hopeful of God’s mercy and not certain of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who know God’s attributes do not presume to be beyond needing His mercy; only the ungrateful and base do so, even with few good deeds.
rows.anchor: those who know the attributes and practices of God do not place themselves beyond the status of being candidates of God’s mercy

rows.speaker: Muḥammad (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly said that no one enters Paradise through deeds alone; he too depends on God’s encompassing mercy.
rows.anchor: Muḥammad (sws) is reported to have said none will enter Paradise because of his own deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer to avoid the unjust people is phrased to convey respect and honour for those on the turrets.
rows.anchor: Its style signifies respect and honour for the people of the turrets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prayer arises as they attend to Paradise’s success and fear Hell’s fate; this conveys their dread and Hell’s horror.
rows.anchor: They will utter these words while being engrossed with the successes of the People of Paradise and dreading the fate of the dwellers of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Lahab, like Abū Jahal, would be recognizable by the people on the turrets among Hell’s leaders.
rows.anchor: Abū Lahab would be recognizable to the people on the turrets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The turret people’s question is rhetorical, meant to humiliate the Paradise dwellers rather than elicit an answer.
rows.anchor: would not be to elicit any answer but to humiliate the dwellers of Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads mā as interrogative rather than negative, creating emphasis; Qur’anic parallels and the next verse’s question support this reading and preserve coherence.
rows.anchor: This creates great emphasis and parallels from the Qur’ān reinforce this interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question recalls Quraysh leaders’ claim that the Prophet’s poor followers were unworthy of God’s choice, while their own affluence made them more eligible.
rows.anchor: they themselves were blessed with affluence and thus were more eligible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to enter Paradise invites its poor dwellers to settle comfortably there, congratulating them and humbling Hell’s people; Joseph’s family were told to enter Egypt while already in his court, meaning reside there.
rows.anchor: stay and take residence in Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition is general divine deprivation, not a sharīʿah legal ban; it resembles God barring the Israelites from the land for forty years.
rows.anchor: In other words, God deprived them of entering that land at any cost for forty years

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dwellers of Paradise could comply, but God has decreed that disbelievers be deprived, so they cannot help fulfill the request.
rows.anchor: it is God Who has decided to deprive them of its fulfilment and hence now they too cannot be of any help

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 51 is a divine insertion explaining why Hell’s people are denied; it turns the scene toward Quraysh’s own circumstances, as an earlier insertion did.
rows.anchor: Through this insertion the discourse relates to the situation of those times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealed religions guide people along the right path in every part of life; those treating worldly life as amusement mock serious truths that oppose their desires.
rows.anchor: Religions are revealed to explain the correct path in every aspect of life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly comfort and apparent freedom from accountability deceived them into thinking life existed only for enjoyment, so they dismissed the Hereafter’s warning as an attack on their freedom.
rows.anchor: When they saw that they were living with such relish and comfort and there was none to question them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s forgetting means ignoring them, the consequence of the verb; God does not literally forget.
rows.anchor: The expression “We shall forget them” means that God will ignore them. In other words, the verb “forget” signifies its consequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether liqāʾ is grammatically annexed to the object or to the place of meeting, the sense is meeting the Lord in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: they forget meeting their Lord on this day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial clause coordinates with the preceding clause, and kamā can express causation as well as comparison, yielding the sense because they denied the revelations.
rows.anchor: and because they continued to deny Our revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun them in the statement about delivering a Book refers to the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: to the Quraysh. The first verse mentions God great favour to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is a favour to Quraysh: God explained with certain knowledge all matters needed for success in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: God in the light of certain knowledge has explained all those matters whose comprehension was necessary for success in this world and the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The descriptions of the Hereafter and its people are not fiction; God’s supreme knowledge makes them certain, and mockers will see them and admit the messengers spoke truly.
rows.anchor: Though they belong to the next world, none should consider them to be fictitious

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite word for knowledge magnifies it: the Book rests on God’s grand, supreme knowledge, so its account is certain.
rows.anchor: In other words this is based on the grand and supreme knowledge of God; all that is said is certain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance describes the Book’s role in this world, while mercy describes the Hereafter’s consequence for those who accept that guidance.
rows.anchor: this book is guidance in this world for people and the consequence of accepting this guidance is mercy in the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for believing carries intention: the verse concerns people who want to believe.
rows.anchor: those who want to believe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Qur’an’s reports concern a veiled future, disbelievers take them for threats and await their manifestation before believing.
rows.anchor: disbelievers think that they are only threats

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The loss means failing to earn virtue in worldly life, whose true value is virtue; such a life becomes a curse and ends in doom, as Sūrah al-ʿAṣr shows.
rows.anchor: his life will become a curse for him and he will be doomed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their fabrication refers to self-invented deities falsely attributed to God, which prove to be a farce.
rows.anchor: “Fabrication” here refers to their concocted deities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous section established polytheism’s baselessness and evil end; verses 54–58 complete the theme by explaining monotheism’s aspects and implications.
rows.anchor: The earlier section concluded on the baseless nature of polytheism and how it will lead people to an evil fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created the heavens and earth and continues to govern the universe; its celestial bodies follow His command, and only its Creator has the right to rule it.
rows.anchor: The night and the day, the sun and the moon, planets and stars, all are subservient to Him and moving in their prescribed paths

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe testifies to its Creator’s benevolence, so people should call on and rely on Him alone in public or private, hope or despair.
rows.anchor: So, people should call Him alone, whether in public or in private and pin all hopes on Him, whether in hope or in despair

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Associating partners with God is rebellion against Him and spreading disorder in the land, which God dislikes.
rows.anchor: If they do so, this is tantamount to being rebellious against God and spreading anarchy in the land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain shows God’s mercy is near: when land is dry and people lose hope, He sends rain to drench it, so only He should be sought in hope or despair.
rows.anchor: It is He Who sends rain after the land gets dry and people lose hope and then drenches the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As rain revives dead land, God will recreate human beings after death and decomposition.
rows.anchor: God will re-create human beings after they die and decompose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Land responds according to its potential: fertile places flourish while barren land yields thorny growth; likewise Qur’anic mercy benefits uncorrupted natures and lights their hearts with faith.
rows.anchor: Those who preserved their natures from getting distorted will obtain any benefit from it and their hearts will light up with the radiance of faith
